title: Delay Alone Does Not Defeat Urgency in a Continuing Trademark Infringement: Calcutta High Court
seo_title: Calcutta HC: Delay Doesn't Bar Urgent IP Relief
meta_description: Calcutta HC exempts Malhotra International from pre-suit mediation in its PANAMA suit, holding delay alone does not negate urgency in ongoing infringement.
bench: Justices Debangsu Basak and Ajay Kumar Gupta
case_name: Malhotra International Pvt. Ltd. v. Respondent(s) (name not confirmed in available reports)
body: A shaving-blade brand that has been on Indian shelves since before the country's own trademark law existed in its present form found itself having to argue, in 2026, that waiting too long to sue does not mean it has lost the right to urgent relief. Malhotra International Pvt. Ltd. says it has sold shaving blades under the mark PANAMA since 1951 and has held a registered trademark for the word since 1954. When it discovered what it says is infringing use of the mark, it filed a suit before the Calcutta High Court's commercial jurisdiction, registered as TEMPAPO-IPD/7/2026, and asked to be exempted from the pre-institution mediation that Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act ordinarily requires before a commercial suit can be filed.

A single judge had refused that exemption, apparently persuaded that the time Malhotra International took before moving to court undercut any claim of urgency. The respondents had argued that they only began using the mark in January 2026 and leaned on the delay to resist being pushed into the usual Section 12A carve-out for cases needing urgent interim relief. Malhotra International appealed, and a Division Bench of Justices Debangsu Basak and Ajay Kumar Gupta set the single judge's order aside on 13 November.

Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 makes pre-institution mediation mandatory for most commercial suits, a position the Supreme Court cemented in Patil Automation v. Rakheja Engineers. The one significant escape hatch is a plaint that genuinely contemplates urgent interim relief, in which case a court can dispense with mediation and let the suit proceed straight to an injunction hearing. Defendants facing trademark suits have increasingly argued that any meaningful delay before filing shows there was no real urgency, and courts have sometimes accepted that argument, as the Calcutta High Court itself did a few weeks earlier when it refused ITC a similar exemption in a counterfeit cigarette dispute, reasoning that an earlier FIR had already weakened ITC's claim to urgency.

The Division Bench in Malhotra International's case drew a different line, building on the Supreme Court's reasoning in its Novenco decision. The Bench held that delay in itself does not negate urgency where the infringement being complained of is a continuing one. A trademark infringement that is still happening on the date of filing is not the same, for urgency purposes, as a one-off act of infringement that occurred years earlier and was simply never acted upon. Where the wrong is ongoing, every day that passes is itself a fresh instance of the harm, and a plaintiff is not disentitled from urgent relief merely because it did not rush to court the moment it first noticed the conduct.

The Bench also pointed out that forcing a plaintiff into mediation in these circumstances could leave it without any real remedy at all, since mediation takes time and a continuing infringer suffers no disadvantage from the process dragging on while the alleged misuse of the mark continues unchecked. On the competing claims about who used the PANAMA mark first and when the respondents say they began using it, the Bench treated these as disputed questions of fact to be gone into at the injunction hearing itself, rather than issues that could be resolved, one way or the other, at the mediation-exemption stage.

Having set aside the refusal, the Division Bench allowed Malhotra International's suit to proceed without pre-institution mediation and directed the Registry to accept the interim applications filed along with the plaint, which means the case can move straight to arguments on interim injunction.

The decision sits alongside a growing body of Calcutta High Court rulings on where the line falls between a plaintiff who has genuinely slept on its rights and one facing an infringement that simply never stopped. Brand owners who wait to gather evidence, negotiate, or exhaust other options before suing should take some comfort from this ruling, provided they can show the infringing conduct is still live on the date they approach the court. Defendants, for their part, will keep arguing that any gap between discovery and filing shows there was no real urgency, and the outcome in a given case will likely turn on whether the court sees the infringement as a continuing wrong or a stale one.
why_it_matters: Section 12A mediation disputes have become a routine opening skirmish in Indian trademark litigation, often delaying the interim injunction a plaintiff actually needs. This ruling gives brand owners facing an ongoing infringement a clearer basis to resist being pushed into mediation purely because they did not sue the moment they discovered the misuse, while reminding defendants that the continuing nature of an infringement, not just the calendar, is what courts will look at when urgency is contested.
card_summary: A Calcutta High Court Bench held that delay in filing a trademark suit does not defeat a claim of urgency where infringement is continuing, exempting Malhotra International from pre-suit mediation.
card_tip: In a trademark suit, delay before filing will not cost a plaintiff its exemption from Section 12A mediation if the infringing use is still ongoing on the filing date.
